source: Seoul National University Korean 2B, Unit 10 · 뭐 먹을래?
pickEn: One exercise at a time — pick where to start.
hintKo: 숫자 키로 고르고, 화살표로 옮기고, Enter로 확인해요.

exercises.blurbEn: Six bowls, six names. The ending tells you what kind of dish it is.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림에 알맞은 음식 이름을 연결해 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Match each picture to the name of the dish.
exercises.noteEn: The book asks you to tick the dishes you have tried, which nothing can mark — so the same twelve become the thing that can be. These six are the 찌개 and the 탕: a 찌개 is thick and eaten from the shared pot, a 탕 is the broth you get a bowl of. Every name here is its ingredient plus that ending.

items.en: kimchi stew
items.why: The everyday stew, and the one that wants kimchi already gone sour — fresh kimchi will not give the broth its depth. Pork belly and tofu go in with it, which is why 삼겹살 turns up later on this page as well.
items.grammar: 김치 + 찌개. Nearly every stew name is built this way: the thing it is made of, then the kind of dish. Once you can hear where the seam is, half the menu reads itself.

items.en: soybean-paste stew
items.why: 된장 is fermented soybean paste, the salty brown one. The stew is what a Korean home eats with rice most nights — closer to a staple than a dish you would order out.
items.grammar: 된장 + 찌개. Worth keeping 된장 apart from 고추장, the red chilli paste, and 간장, soy sauce — 장 is the family word for all three.

items.en: soft-tofu stew
items.why: 순두부 is tofu that was never pressed, so it comes out of the pot in soft curds rather than cubes. It arrives still boiling and a raw egg is usually cracked into it at the table.
items.grammar: 순 + 두부 + 찌개. 순 means unmixed or pure, the same 순 as in 순수하다. So 순두부 is tofu in its first state, before anything is done to it.

items.en: pork-bone potato stew
items.why: Pork spine simmered for hours until the meat gives, with potato, perilla leaf and greens. A late-night dish — the sort of thing eaten sitting on plastic stools after work.
items.grammar: 감자 + 탕. 감자 is potato, though there is a long argument that the 감자 here is a cut of the pig rather than the vegetable. Either way the ending 탕 marks it as the long-simmered kind of soup.

items.en: spicy fish stew
items.why: Whatever fish was fresh, boiled up with chilli, radish and 쑥갓. Often what happens to the bones and head after the good cuts have been served as 회.
items.grammar: 맵다 → 매운 + 탕. This is the one dish on the page whose name starts with an adjective in its modifier form — 맵다 loses its 다 and takes -운, exactly as it does in 매운 음식.

items.en: ox-bone soup
items.why: Ox bones boiled long enough that the broth turns milky white and tastes of almost nothing until you salt it yourself at the table. The salt, spring onion and rice are the point — it arrives deliberately plain.
items.grammar: 설렁 + 탕. Unlike the other five this name does not come apart into words you already know; it is worth learning whole. Note it is 탕 and not 찌개 — you get your own bowl.

exercises.blurbEn: Noodles and grilled meat — six more names to put to the picture.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림에 알맞은 음식 이름을 연결해 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Match each picture to the name of the dish.
exercises.noteEn: The other six from the same page. Three noodle dishes and three ways with beef and pork — and all six names say plainly what is done to the food, once you can hear the pieces.

items.en: cold noodles
items.why: Buckwheat noodles in an icy broth, eaten in the heat of summer. Scissors come with it, because the noodles are too long and too chewy to bite through politely.
items.grammar: 냉(冷) + 면(麵), cold + noodle, both Sino-Korean. The same 냉 is in 냉장고, the cold-storage box, and the same 면 is in 라면.

items.en: knife-cut noodles
items.why: The dough is rolled out and cut into strips by hand, so the noodles come out uneven and the starch clouds the broth. Anchovy or clam stock, and a rainy day.
items.grammar: 칼 + 국수, knife + noodles. This is the native Korean word for noodles; 면 is the Sino-Korean one. Both mean the same thing, and which one a dish uses is just which language its name came from.

items.en: spicy mixed noodles
items.why: No broth — the noodles are tossed in gochujang, vinegar and sugar until every strand is red. Served cold, usually with a boiled egg and cucumber on top.
items.grammar: 비비다 → 비빔 + 국수. 비비다 is to rub or mix, and 비빔 is the noun made from it. The same 비빔 gives 비빔밥, mixed rice, which is the dish this one is named after.

items.en: grilled pork belly
items.why: Grilled at the table on a slanted pan so the fat runs off, then cut with scissors and wrapped in lettuce with garlic and ssamjang. The most sociable food in the country.
items.grammar: 삼(三) + 겹 + 살, three + layer + flesh. The name is a description of the cut: lean and fat in three visible bands. 오겹살, five layers, is the same cut with the skin left on.

items.en: grilled minced ribs
items.why: Rib meat taken off the bone, chopped, seasoned and pressed back into a patty before grilling. It began as court food, for eating ribs without having to pick them up.
items.grammar: 떡 + 갈비, rice cake + ribs. Nothing in it is rice cake — 떡 is there for the shape, because the patty is patted flat the way 떡 is.

items.en: braised short ribs
items.why: Short ribs simmered slowly in soy sauce with radish, carrot, chestnut and jujube until the meat comes away from the bone. Holiday food — 설날 and 추석.
items.grammar: 갈비 + 찜. 찜 is the steamed or braised method, from 찌다, and it is what separates this from 갈비구이, the grilled version. The ending is the cooking, not the ingredient.

exercises.blurbEn: Five tastes, five different endings — and two irregulars hiding.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 알맞은 단어를 골라 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue using the word from the box.
exercises.noteEn: Pick the dictionary form; the blank fills with the shape that sentence needs, and no two sentences need the same one. Watch 맵다 and 쓰다 — both are irregular, and both look perfectly ordinary until an ending starting with a vowel is put on them.

items.en: A: The soup is a bit salty. — B: I think I put in too much salt.
items.why: B names the cause — 소금, salt — so A must be saying it is salty. 국 is the thin soup that comes with a Korean meal, as against 찌개, the thick one.
items.grammar: 짜다 → 짜요. A regular ㅏ stem: 짜 + 아요 collapses to 짜요, since the vowel is already there.

lines.ko: 소금을 좀 많이 넣은 것 같아요.

items.en: A: Shall we have tteokbokki? — B: I can’t really eat spicy food.
items.why: 떡볶이 is the rice cakes in red sauce sold on every street corner, so B is turning it down for the obvious reason. 잘 못 먹어요 is the polite way to say it: not "I hate it" but "I am not good at eating it".
items.grammar: 맵다 → 매운. ㅂ-irregular: before a vowel ending the ㅂ becomes 우, so 맵 + 은 gives 매운. This is the modifier form, which is why it stands in front of 음식 rather than ending the sentence.

items.en: A: The coffee is too bitter, I can’t drink it. — B: Then put in some milk or sugar.
items.why: B offers milk or sugar, which only answers bitterness. -겠- in 못 마시겠어요 softens it to "I don’t think I can" rather than a flat refusal.
items.grammar: 쓰다 → 써서. ㅡ-irregular: the ㅡ drops before a vowel ending and there is no syllable in front to take a vowel from, so it defaults to 어. -아/어서 gives the reason: bitter, and therefore undrinkable.

items.en: A: This cake is good, do try some. — B: Ah, I’m on a diet at the moment, so I don’t eat sweet things.
items.why: A offers cake, B is dieting — so the thing being avoided is sweetness. 드시다 is the honorific of 먹다, which is why A uses it when offering food to someone else.
items.grammar: 달다 → 단. A ㄹ stem drops its ㄹ before ㄴ: 달 + ㄴ = 단. Same shape as 만들다 → 만든 and 살다 → 산. 것 turns the modifier into "sweet things".

lines.ko: 이 케이크 맛있는데 좀 드셔 보세요.
아, 제가 요즘 다이어트 중이에요. 그래서 {} 것을 안 먹어요.

items.en: A: How is the naengmyeon? — B: They put in a lot of vinegar, so it’s a bit sour.
items.why: 식초 is vinegar, which leaves only one taste it could be. 냉면 is the cold noodle dish from 연습 2, and vinegar is what people add to it at the table.
items.grammar: 시다 → 시어요. ㅣ + 어요 normally contracts to 셔요 and you will hear 셔요 constantly, but the book prints the uncontracted 시어요 here — both are correct.

exercises.blurbEn: What makes a restaurant good — and which particle the word takes.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 알맞은 단어를 골라 문장을 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each sentence using the word from the box.
exercises.noteEn: The book prints 이/가 after the blank and leaves you to pick the noun. Here the particle comes with it, because choosing between 이 and 가 is the part with a rule: 이 after a final consonant, 가 after a vowel. Two of the five words are never needed — the book gives you more than the sentences use.

items.en: This restaurant has a nice atmosphere, so it would be a good place for a date.
items.why: Nothing about the food or the price — the reason given is that it suits a date, and that is what 분위기 covers: the feel of a place, its lighting and quiet and how it makes you want to behave.
items.grammar: 분위기 ends in the vowel ㅣ, so the subject particle is 가. -아/어서 gives the reason, and -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 at the end is a guess: it would probably be good.
items.stemKo: 이 식당은 {} 좋아서 데이트할 때 가면 좋을 것 같아요.

items.en: This restaurant has good service. The staff are very kind.
items.why: The second sentence explains the first: the staff are kind, so what is good is the service. 서비스 in Korean also stretches to mean something given free — a dish 서비스로 is on the house.
items.grammar: 서비스 ends in the vowel ㅡ, so again 가. Note 직원들 — 들 marks the plural, which Korean uses only when it matters.
items.stemKo: 이 식당은 {} 좋아요. 직원들이 아주 친절해요.

items.en: This restaurant is easy to get to. It’s a five-minute walk from the subway station.
items.why: Five minutes from the station is about getting there, not about the food, so it is 교통. 편리하다 is the word for convenient in this sense — easy to reach.
items.grammar: 교통 ends in the consonant ㅇ, so the particle is 이 rather than 가. 걸어서 is 걷다 with -아/어서: the ㄷ turns to ㄹ before a vowel, the same ㄷ-irregular as 듣다 → 들어요.
items.stemKo: 이 식당은 {} 편리해요. 지하철역에서 걸어서 5분 걸려요.

exercises.blurbEn: Out of this lot, which one wins — and what is “this lot” called?
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book photographs the group and leaves the whole phrase blank. There are no photographs here, so the members are named instead — the four fruits in the picture become 사과 · 딸기 · 오렌지 · 포도, and you supply what they add up to. 중에 and 중에서 are both correct, which is what the brackets in the title mean, so the wrong answers are wrong for other reasons: 에서 wants a place, and the noun in front of 중에서 has to be the whole group rather than the one that wins.

items.en: A: Which fruit do you like best? — B: I like strawberries.
items.why: B answers 딸기, and 딸기 is one of the four in the picture — so the group being asked about is what all four have in common: 과일. Ask 딸기 중에서 and you have asked which strawberry, out of one strawberry.
items.grammar: N 중에서 marks the set you are choosing from and 뭘 is what you pick out of it. 과일에서 would make the fruit a place — 에서 is for 서울에서, 학교에서, somewhere you can actually be.

items.en: A: Which food tastes best? — B: Bulgogi does.
items.why: Four dishes, and B picks one of them. What the four have in common is that they are all 음식, so that is the group. Note 뭐가 rather than 뭘: 맛있다 takes no object, so the thing being asked about is the subject of the sentence.
items.grammar: 음식 중에서 뭐가 제일 맛있어요 — the set, then the question word, then 제일. 제일 and 가장 are interchangeable here; 가장 is a shade more formal and turns up in writing more often.

items.en: A: Which sport are you best at? — B: I’m good at basketball.
items.why: Football, basketball, baseball, swimming — B answers with 농구, one of them, so the set is 운동. 잘해요 is 잘 + 해요, and what you are good at takes 를/을: 농구를 잘해요.
items.grammar: 운동 중에서 뭘 제일 잘해요. 뭘 is 무엇을 shortened, which is why it fits a verb that takes an object. 운동에서 would be reaching for the place particle on something that is not a place.

items.en: A: Who speaks Korean best in our class? — B: Akira does.
items.why: The three names are the classmates in the picture, so the group is 우리 반 학생 — the students of our class. And 누가 rather than 뭘, because the answer is a person.
items.grammar: The group can be a whole phrase, not just one noun: 우리 반 학생 중에서. 우리 반에서 would also be good Korean — that is the class taken as a place, and it is what 연습 2 asks for — but 우리 반 학생에서 is neither, because 학생 is not somewhere you can be.

items.en: A: Which month of the year is the hottest? — B: August is.
items.why: The chart in the book plots twelve months and B picks one of them, so the set the twelve add up to is 1년 — the year itself. 몇 월 asks which month, and the answer names it with a Sino-Korean number: 8월, 팔월.
items.grammar: Stretches of time behave like anything else countable: 하루 중에서, 일주일 중에서, 1년 중에서. 1년에서 is not Korean for this — 에서 on a length of time only works in a range, 1년에서 2년까지.

lines.ko: 민수 씨 {} 누가 제일 키가 커요?

example.en: A: Who is the tallest in your family, Minsu? — B: My younger sibling is.

exercises.blurbEn: Now you ask the question: the place takes 에서, and the adjective bends.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Here the book has you write A’s whole question out of a place and an adjective — 서울 / 크다 becomes 서울에서 제일 큰 시장이 어디예요? Two decisions are left to you and the fixed words are printed: which particle the place takes, and what shape the adjective goes into in front of a noun. 중에서 is wrong on every row here, and that is why the two 연습 sit side by side — a group of things takes 중에서, a place you look inside takes 에서.

items.en: A: Which is the highest mountain in the world? — B: Mount Everest is.
items.why: The label hands you 세계 and 높다 and B names the mountain; the question is the part missing. 세계 is a place — the world — so it takes 에서, and the question ends 어디예요 even though the answer comes back as a name.
items.grammar: 높다 is an adjective, so in front of a noun it takes -(으)ㄴ: 높 + 은 = 높은. 높는 is the -는 that verbs take and an adjective never does, and 높이 is the adverb, high up.

items.en: A: Which is the biggest island in Korea? — B: Jeju is the biggest island.
items.why: B says 가장 큰 섬이에요 and hands you the answer’s shape while doing it — 가장 is 제일 in other words. So A asked which island is biggest, and 한국 is where to look for it.
items.grammar: 크다 → 큰. The stem 크 ends in a vowel, so the ending is a bare ㄴ tucked underneath rather than 은: 크 + ㄴ = 큰. 크은 spells out an 으 that a vowel stem never takes, and 크는 is again the verb ending.

lines.ko: 강남 근처가 제일 복잡한 것 같아요.

items.en: A: Which is the most crowded part of Seoul? — B: Somewhere around Gangnam, I’d say.
items.why: B hedges with -(으)ㄴ 것 같아요 — it seems to be — instead of naming it flatly, which is what you do when you are not certain. 곳 is the general word for a place, and it is what the question needs when the answer is an area rather than one building.
items.grammar: 복잡하다 → 복잡한. Every 하다 adjective goes this way: 하 + ㄴ = 한. 복잡하는 is the verb ending again, and 복잡해요 is the finished 해요 form, which can end a sentence but cannot sit in front of a noun.

items.en: A: Which restaurant near the school is the best? — B: Seoul Restaurant is.
items.why: 학교 근처 is a place built out of two nouns — the school, and the area around it — and it takes 에서 as one unit. B answers with a name, 서울식당, the sort of 맛집 this whole unit is about.
items.grammar: 맛있다 → 맛있는, and this is the one worth memorising: it is an adjective, but it is built on 있다, and 있다 takes -는 in front of a noun. 맛있은 is the regular adjective ending and it is wrong here. Same for 맛없다 → 맛없는 and 재미있다 → 재미있는.

items.en: A: Who is the most popular person in our class? — B: Hmm, Kelly, I think.
items.why: 글쎄요 buys a moment before an answer you are not sure of, and 것 같아요 finishes the hedge — both are all over this unit. The question ends 누구예요 rather than 어디예요, because this is the one row whose answer is a person.
items.grammar: 많다 → 많은, a plain adjective, and 많이 is its adverb. The place is 우리 반에서 and not 우리 반 중에서: 중에서 picks out of a set of things, and 반 is one class rather than several. 연습 1 put the students in the set instead — 우리 반 학생 중에서 — which is the same idea from the other side.

example.en: A: Which is the biggest market in Seoul? — B: Namdaemun Market is the biggest.

exercises.blurbEn: I and you, in 반말 — and 나 changes shape depending on what follows.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 빈칸에 알맞은 단어를 골라 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each dialogue using the word from the box as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Twelve words in the box, six blanks and the worked example — so half the box is never used, exactly as the book prints it. The whole page turns on two shape changes: 나 becomes 내 in front of 가 and in front of whatever it owns, and 너 becomes 네 in the same two places. Everywhere else — 는, 를, 도, 한테 — they keep their own shape.

items.en: A: Call me when class finishes. — B: Sure, I’ll call.
items.why: A is the one asking to be called, so the call comes to A — 나한테. B agrees with 그래 and -(으)ㄹ게, which is the ending for promising to do something because the other person wants it.
items.grammar: 나 + 한테. 한테 is the spoken word for to a person; 에게 is its written twin and 께 the honorific one. 나 keeps its own shape here — it only turns into 내 in front of 가 or a noun.

items.en: A: Let’s have lunch together. — B: I’ve already eaten, though.
items.why: B turns the invitation down by contrasting themselves with A: 나는, as for me. The sentence stops at -는데 rather than finishing, and that unfinished feel is what makes it a soft refusal instead of a flat no.
items.grammar: 나 + 는, the topic particle. 내는 does not exist — 내 is 나 + 가 or 나 followed by what it owns, and nothing else.

items.en: A: Whose book is this? — B: Oh, that’s my book.
items.why: 누구 책 asks whose, so the answer has to name an owner. Watch 이거 and 그거 as well: the book is by A, so A calls it 이거, this one, and B calls it 그거, that one by you.
items.grammar: 나 + 의 contracts to 내, and that is the form that stands in front of the thing owned: 내 책, 내 친구, 내 생일. 저 does the same in 존댓말 — 제 책.

items.en: A: I called you earlier — you didn’t know? — B: Did you? I left my phone at home today.
items.why: This is item 1 the other way round: A did the calling and B was called, so it is 너한테. A’s line already contains 내가, which is the shape 나 takes in front of 가 — the pair is worth reading together.
items.grammar: 너 + 한테. Like 나, 너 keeps its own shape in front of 한테; it becomes 네 only in front of 가 or a noun it owns.

lines.ko: 그랬어? 오늘 휴대폰을 집에 놓고 왔어.

items.en: A: Is this yours? — B: Yes, it’s mine.
items.why: B claims it with 내 거, mine, so what A asked about was 네 거, yours. 거 is 것 worn down in speech, so 네 거 is literally your thing.
items.grammar: 너 + 의 → 네. And here is the trap: this 네 is spelled exactly like the 네 that means yes. Speakers pronounce it 니 to keep them apart — which is also why 네가 comes out as 니가 — but 네 is what gets written.

items.en: A: It’s Nana’s birthday, so I’m going over to hers tonight. You’re coming too, right? — B: Yes, I’m coming too.
items.why: A ends with 너도 — you too — and B answers with the same particle pointed back: 나도. A’s -지? is asking for confirmation of something already taken for granted, so all B has to do is agree.
items.grammar: 나 + 도. 도 replaces 은/는 and 이/가 rather than stacking on top of them: 나도 갈 거야, never 나는도 or 내가도.

lines.ko: 오늘 나나 생일이라서 저녁에 나나 집에 갈 거야. 너도 갈 거지?

example.en: A: I don’t really get the grammar we did today. — B: I’ll teach you.

exercises.blurbEn: Take the 요 off — and find out what was hiding under it.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 반말로 바꿔 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Change the sentences into 반말 as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book gives you a ruled line to write on; here the three forms are offered and one of them is right. Dropping 요 is only the first half of the job. The 아/어 underneath has to be the correct one, 이에요/예요 becomes 이야/야 rather than losing a syllable, -(으)ㄹ까요 and -아/어요 as a suggestion go somewhere else entirely, and 저/제 has to become 나/내 wherever it appears.

items.en: That restaurant has a nice atmosphere.
items.why: The gentlest case: 요 comes off and nothing else moves. 분위기 is the word from the 어휘 pages of this unit — the feel of a place rather than its food.
items.grammar: 좋아요 → 좋아. Taking 요 off leaves the 아/어 exposed, so it has to be the right one: 좋 has ㅗ in it, so the ending is 아. 좋어 is the same mistake as writing 좋어요.

items.en: The naengmyeon is a bit spicy.
items.why: 냉면 and 맵다 are both from this unit’s vocabulary, and 맵다 is one of the two irregulars the 어휘 page drilled. Here the irregularity is already done for you in the polite form — the job is to keep it.
items.grammar: 매워요 → 매워. 맵다 is ㅂ-irregular: before a vowel the ㅂ turns into 우, so 맵 + 어 gives 매워. 맵어 is what the rule would give if the ㅂ stayed, and it never does.

items.en: I exercise every morning.
items.why: Two things change, and the first is easy to forget: 저 is the humble I that belongs with 요, so in 반말 it has to become 나. Leave 저는 in and the sentence is half polite and half not.
items.grammar: 저는 → 나는, and 해요 → 해. 하다 takes 여 rather than 아/어, and 하 + 여 contracts to 해 — which is why 하어 is never a step on the way. 내는 does not exist at all: 내 is only 나 + 가 or 나 in front of a noun.

items.en: I’ll watch a film after I finish my homework.
items.why: A plan, stated with -(으)ㄹ 거예요. -고 나서 is what makes the order explicit: the homework is finished first, and only then the film.
items.grammar: 거예요 → 거야. This is the one that catches people, because it is not a matter of dropping 요: 거예요 is 거 + 이에요, and 이에요 becomes 이야, which after the vowel of 거 is just 야. 거예 is what dropping 요 alone would leave, and it is not a word.

items.en: The exam won’t be difficult.
items.why: The same 거예요 as item 4, but this time it is a guess about the future rather than a plan — -(으)ㄹ 거예요 does both. The negative sits earlier, in 어렵지 않다, and is not touched by the change.
items.grammar: 않을 거예요 → 않을 거야. Only the very end of the sentence carries the politeness, so that is the only part that moves — A/V-지 않다 stays exactly as it is.

items.en: A friend lost my camera.
items.why: 제 is the humble my, so it goes the same way 저 does: 내. The friend is the subject and the camera the object, which is why 친구 takes 가 and 카메라 takes 를 — the sentence is not about who owns it but about who lost it.
items.grammar: 제 → 내, and 잃어버렸어요 → 잃어버렸어. 나 카메라 is wrong for the same reason 저 카메라 is: in front of a noun it owns, 나 has to become 내. And the past marker 았/었 is always followed by 어, never 아.

items.en: These clothes are ones I bought last year.
items.why: 거예요 for the third time, and here the 거 is not a plan or a guess but a plain fact: V-(으)ㄴ 거예요 explains what something is. 산 is 사다 in its past modifier form.
items.grammar: 산 거예요 → 산 거야. Whatever comes in front of 거 — 볼, 않을, 산 — the ending behaves the same, because the politeness lives in 이에요 and nowhere else.

items.en: Tomorrow is my friend’s birthday.
items.why: Two owners in a row — my friend’s birthday — and Korean stacks them without any particle at all: 내 친구 생일. 제 has to go the way 저 does, exactly as in item 6, and then the sentence ends in a noun, which is where the second change lives.
items.grammar: 이에요 → 이야, and which of 이야 or 야 you get depends on the noun in front: 생일 ends in a consonant, so it is 생일이야. A noun ending in a vowel takes the bare 야 — 친구야, 나나야.

items.en: There really are a lot of people at the cinema.
items.why: -네요 is the ending for saying out loud what you have only just noticed, and it keeps that job in 반말 — it simply loses its 요. Say 많아 instead and the surprise goes out of the sentence.
items.grammar: 많네요 → 많네. -네 attaches straight to the stem with no 으 in between, so 많으네 is one syllable too many. Compare -(으)면 and -(으)ㄹ 거야, which do take the 으 after a consonant.

items.en: Let’s go for a coffee together.
items.why: 같이 gives it away: this 가요 is not a statement but a suggestion, and a suggestion in 반말 is not 가 but 가자. The English let’s is the giveaway in both languages.
items.grammar: 가요 → 가자. -아/어요 does double duty as statement and suggestion, and only the suggestion turns into -자. 갑시다 is the same suggestion in the formal style, so it is moving away from 반말 rather than towards it.

items.en: Call me when you get there.
items.why: A request, so both halves have to come down at once: the humble 저한테 becomes 나한테, and the polite 주세요 becomes 줘. This is the same 나한테 that 연습 1 asked for in its first dialogue.
items.grammar: 주세요 → 줘. V-아/어 주다 is asking someone to do something for you, and the 반말 of it is the plain 아/어 form of 주다: 주 + 어 contracts to 줘. 줘요 is the 해요체 version, one step short.

items.en: Don’t be late tomorrow.
items.why: Telling someone not to do something. The negative command is V-지 말다, and 마세요 is its polite form — so the 반말 is the shortest form of the same verb.
items.grammar: 마세요 → 마. 말다 loses its ㄹ here, which is why it is 마 and not 말. 말아요 is the 해요체 form of the same thing, so it is still carrying its 요.

items.en: I’ll order by phone.
items.why: 제가 is the humble I as a subject, so it becomes 내가 — the same 내가 the worked example of 연습 1 used. -(으)ㄹ게 is a promise: I will do it, since you want it done.
items.grammar: 주문할게요 → 주문할게. It is pronounced 주문할께, which is why 께 looks so plausible, but the spelling is 게. 나가 is not a form of 나 at all — in front of 가 it has to be 내.

items.en: Shall we go to the mountains at the weekend?
items.why: A suggestion put as a question — shall we? — and it stays a question in 반말. Item 10 was the same idea stated rather than asked, which is why that one became 가자 and this one does not.
items.grammar: 갈까요 → 갈까. -(으)ㄹ까요 loses its 요 and nothing else, so the question mark stays too. 갑시다 answers the suggestion in the formal style instead of asking it in the plain one.

items.en: It’s really cold today, isn’t it?
items.why: -지요 checks something you already believe — isn’t it? — and 반말 keeps the checking and drops the 요. It is the same -지 that 연습 1 item 6 used in 너도 갈 거지?
items.grammar: 춥지요 → 춥지. -지 goes on the plain stem 춥-, not on the 아/어 form, so the ㅂ-irregular never gets a chance to fire: 추워 is 춥 + 어, and there is no 어 here. That is why it is 춥지 and not 추워지.

example.en: The bibimbap is good. → the same thing said to a friend.

exercises.blurbEn: Answer the question — in the register it was asked in.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book leaves B’s line blank for you to fill however you like, and prints one model answer in the key. That cannot be marked, so the model answer is offered here against two replies that answer the question but get something else wrong — the register slips back into 존댓말, or the tense does not match what was asked. Any polite word gives it away, 네 included: the 반말 yes is 응.

items.en: A: Are you going to the restaurant now? — B: Yes, I’m going now.
items.why: A yes-or-no question about a plan, so the answer confirms the plan in the same words: 갈 거야. Both wrong answers say the right thing and then betray themselves with one polite word.
items.grammar: 네 is the 존댓말 yes and belongs with 갈 거예요; the 반말 pair is 응 and 갈 거야. Mixing them — 네 with 거야, or 응 with 거예요 — is the commonest slip there is, because the two halves are learned separately.

items.en: A: Shall we go and see a film at the weekend? — B: Sure, let’s go.
items.why: A suggests with -(으)ㄹ까, and agreeing to a suggestion means making it: 가자. 갈까 would be handing the question straight back, which answers nothing.
items.grammar: 그래 is the 반말 agreement — 좋아 works too — and 가자 is the -자 suggestion 연습 2 item 10 drilled. 가요 is that same suggestion in 해요체, so it does not belong after 그래.

items.en: A: What did you do yesterday? — B: I did my homework at home.
items.why: 어제 puts the question in the past, so an answer about what you are going to do does not answer it, however good its 반말 is. 뭐 했어 is 무엇을 했어 worn down in speech.
items.grammar: 했어요 → 했어. The past 았/었 is already inside 했 — 하 + 였 — and the politeness is the 요 on the end, so that is all that comes off.

items.en: A: What are you doing after class today? — B: I’m going for lunch.
items.why: 오늘 … 끝나고 asks about what has not happened yet, even though 뭐 해 is in the present — Korean uses the plain present for the near future all the time. So the answer looks ahead: 갈 거야.
items.grammar: -(으)러 가다 is going in order to do something, and the 으 appears because 먹 ends in a consonant: 먹으러, but 마시러. The tense sits at the very end of the sentence, in 갈 거야.

items.en: A: When’s your birthday? — B: My birthday is the 20th of September.
items.why: A asks in 반말, so answering in 존댓말 would be the odd thing to do. The third answer is the interesting one: it starts in 반말 with 내 and finishes in 존댓말 with 이에요, and a sentence cannot be both.
items.grammar: 제 → 내 and 이에요 → 이야, the two changes of 연습 2 item 8 in one line. 며칠 asks which day of the month; the answer reads 구월 이십일 — Sino-Korean numbers for both the month and the date.

lines.ko: 이 근처에 서점이 어디에 있는지 알아?

example.en: A: Do you know where there’s a bookshop near here? — B: Yes, next to the subway station.

exercises.blurbEn: Ten questions to ask a friend — some of them start out very formal indeed.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 반말로 바꿔서 이야기해 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Change the following sentences into 반말 as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: In the book this is spoken practice with a partner; what can be marked is the transformation itself, so that is what is offered here. Every row puts the same three registers side by side — 반말, 해요체 and the formal 합니다체 — and only the first is asked for. Item 6 is the one that is not just an ending: 성함 and 되십니까 are honorifics, and 반말 has no use for either.

items.en: Where do you live now?
items.why: The starting point is as formal as Korean gets: 합니다체 with the honorific 시 on top. 반말 drops both at once, which is why the distance between the two versions feels so large.
items.grammar: 사십니까 → 살아. Take the honorific 시 out and you are back to 살다, and 살 + 아 = 살아. The ㄹ stays here because 아 is a vowel — it is 십니까 and 습니다 that make a ㄹ disappear.

items.en: Are you enjoying life in Korea?
items.why: A 해요체 question this time, so only the 요 has to go. Asking a question in 반말 is done with the tone of voice alone — nothing is added to mark it.
items.grammar: 재미있어요 → 재미있어. 재미있다 is built on 있다, the same 있다 that made 맛있는 take -는 in the previous grammar point. Here it is the plain 어 form and behaves normally.

items.en: What kind of food do you like?
items.why: Worth putting beside 연습 2 item 1: that one was 좋아, this one is 좋아해. 좋다 is an adjective — it is good — and 좋아하다 is a verb, to like, which is why this sentence can take 음식을 as its object.
items.grammar: 좋아해요 → 좋아해. 좋아하다 is a 하다 verb, so its plain form is 좋아해, from 하 + 여. 무슨 asks which kind, as against 어느, which asks which one of a known few.

items.en: Korean study is hard going, isn’t it?
items.why: -지요 is the ending that assumes the answer — it must be hard, mustn’t it — and 반말 keeps that and drops the 요, exactly as in 연습 2 item 15. The other two forms ask the question flat out instead of taking the answer for granted.
items.grammar: 힘들지요 → 힘들지. N 때문에 gives the cause: because of studying Korean. The ㄹ of 힘들다 survives in front of -지 and disappears before ㄴ, ㅂ and ㅅ — which is why the formal form on offer is 힘듭니까 and not 힘들습니까.

items.en: What time are you going home, roughly?
items.why: The 거예요 → 거야 change again, this time inside a question. -쯤 is the about-ish suffix — 몇 시쯤 is around what time — and it makes the question easier to answer.
items.grammar: 갈 거예요 → 갈 거야. 겁니다 and 겁니까 are 거 + 입니다 squeezed together, the formal style of the same ending, so they are the opposite direction from 반말.

items.en: What’s your name?
items.why: The one row where the words themselves change and not just the ending. 성함 is the honorific word for a name and 어떻게 되십니까 is the honorific way of asking for one; to a friend both are simply 이름이 뭐야. Keeping 성함 and dropping the politeness would be the strangest sentence on the page.
items.grammar: Honorific nouns come in pairs with plain ones: 성함 / 이름, 연세 / 나이, 진지 / 밥, 분 / 사람. They travel with the honorific 시 — which is what the 셔 in 되셔 is — and 반말 uses neither.

items.en: Shall we have lunch together today?
items.why: A suggestion asked as a question, like 연습 2 item 14, so it stays a question and only loses its 요. 먹읍시다 says the same thing but as a formal proposal, which is a strange thing to say to a friend about lunch.
items.grammar: 먹을까요 → 먹을까. Both -(으)ㄹ까 and -(으)ㅂ시다 take the 으 after a consonant stem, which is why it is 먹을까 but 갈까, 먹읍시다 but 갑시다.

items.en: How are you feeling today?
items.why: 어때요 is so worn down that there is not much left to take off — just the 요. 기분 is how you feel rather than what you think, so this is asking after someone’s mood.
items.grammar: 어때요 → 어때. 어때 is 어떠하다 collapsed twice over, which is why the formal 어떻습니까 looks like a different word altogether. Both come from the same stem.

items.en: Don’t be late tomorrow morning.
items.why: The negative command from 연습 2 item 12, met again — the book repeats it deliberately, because 마세요 → 마 loses more than it looks like it should. 마십시오 is the formal version, the one on signs and announcements.
items.grammar: 마세요 → 마. V-지 말다 makes the negative command, and 말다 drops its ㄹ in front of these endings: 마세요, 마십시오, 마.

items.en: Let’s meet at the weekend.
items.why: -(으)ㅂ시다 is a suggestion in the formal style, and the plain-style suggestion is -자. So this row and item 7 are the two halves of the same idea: 만납시다 is stated, 먹을까요 is asked.
items.grammar: 만납시다 → 만나자. The three suggestions to keep apart are 만나자 (반말), 만나요 (해요체) and 만납시다 (합니다체) — and 만납시다 is not as polite as it sounds, which is why 만나요 is the safer one with a stranger.

example.en: Where do you live? — the same question put to a friend.

exercises.blurbEn: One phone call, start to finish, taken down into 반말.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 다음을 반말로 바꿔 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Change the following conversation into 반말 as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book prints the call twice — once in 존댓말 and once as a frame with fifteen blanks — and 정우’s first line is filled in as the [보기]. The frame is kept here, in order, with one change: a turn of two sentences is split into two rows, because a row draws at most two groups of buttons. The polite version of each line is printed above the row it belongs to. Note what happens to the names as well: 스티븐 씨 becomes plain 스티븐, and 스티븐 씨가 becomes 네가.

items.en: Yes, it’s fine.
items.why: Two words, two decisions, and the first one is the one people forget: 네 is the polite yes and has no place in a 반말 answer. 응 is what goes there — 어 does the same job.
items.grammar: 괜찮아요 → 괜찮아. With the 요 gone the 아/어 is exposed, and 괜찮 has ㅏ in its last syllable, so it takes 아. 예 is 네 in its more formal dress, so it is the wrong direction twice over.

items.en: I was in the middle of my homework.
items.why: V-는 중이다 is being in the middle of doing something, and 이었어요 puts it in the past: Steven was doing homework when the phone rang. 중이야 would move it into the present and answer a different question.
items.grammar: 중이었어요 → 중이었어. The chain is 중 + 이다 + 었 + 어요, and only the last piece is polite. 이었 is what 이다 becomes in the past after a consonant; after a vowel it contracts, as in 친구였어.

items.phraseKo: 스티븐 씨, 한국 전통 음악 좋아하지요?
items.en: Steven, you like traditional Korean music, don’t you?
items.why: Jeongwoo is checking something he already believes, which is what -지요 does, and 반말 keeps the checking. Note the name: 씨 comes off, because 씨 is politeness of the same kind as 요.
items.grammar: 좋아하지요 → 좋아하지. 좋아하시지 keeps the honorific 시, which is for someone above you — using it on a friend inside a 반말 sentence pulls in two directions at once.

items.en: Yes, I like it.
items.why: The same 응 as item 1, and the verb from 연습 4 item 3. Steven is answering a -지 question, which is why a bare 응 is enough — he only has to confirm what was already assumed.
items.grammar: 좋아해요 → 좋아해. 하다 takes 여 and 하 + 여 contracts to 해, so 하어 is a form that never exists — not here and not in 해요, 했어, 해서.

items.en: But why do you ask?
items.why: 왜요 is a whole question in two syllables — why? — and taking the 요 off leaves 왜 standing on its own, which is exactly how it works in 반말. 그런데 is the but that changes the subject rather than contradicting.
items.grammar: 왜요 → 왜. 요 can be added to almost any word to make it polite without changing anything else — 왜요, 언제요, 저요 — and it comes off the same way. 왜 is not a noun, so 이야/야 has nothing to attach to.

items.phraseKo: 국립국악원에서 하는 외국인을 위한 국악 수업이 있는데 스티븐 씨가 좋아할 것 같아서 전화했어요.

lines.ko: 국립국악원에서 하는 외국인을 위한 국악 수업이 있는데 {} 좋아할 것 같아서 {}.

items.en: There’s a gugak class for foreigners at the National Gugak Center, and I thought you’d like it, so I called.
items.why: The long one. 스티븐 씨가 is Jeongwoo talking about the person he is talking to, in the third person — which is polite Korean and quite normal. In 반말 you address them directly instead: 네가.
items.grammar: 네가 is 너 + 가, and it is the standard form even though everyone pronounces it 니가 to keep it apart from 내가. 너가 is what that pronunciation gets written as, and it is not standard. -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is the guess: I thought you would probably like it.

items.en: Really? What day is it on?
items.why: Two questions in one turn. 그래요? is surprise — is that so? — and 하는데요? is the ending that leaves a question hanging so the other person fills it in. Both simply lose their 요.
items.grammar: 하는데요 → 하는데. -는데 can end a sentence like this, and 하는지 cannot: -는지 needs a verb after it to hold it up, as in 어디에 있는지 알아 in the [보기] of 연습 3.

items.phraseKo: 토요일에 하는데 자세한 것은 전화해서 물어보세요. 문자로 전화번호 보내 줄게요.

lines.ko: 토요일에 하는데 자세한 것은 전화해서 {}. 문자로 전화번호 보내 {}.

items.en: It’s on Saturdays. Ring them and ask for the details — I’ll text you the number.
items.why: Jeongwoo tells Steven to do one thing and promises to do another, so the two blanks are two different endings: a command and a promise. -(으)ㄹ게 is always about the speaker, which is why it can only be Jeongwoo who sends the text.
items.grammar: 물어보세요 → 물어봐: 보 + 아 contracts to 봐. 줄게요 → 줄게, and the 게 is spelled with ㄱ even though it is pronounced 께 — the same trap as 주문할게 in 연습 2.

items.en: Yes — thanks.
items.why: The call closes the way it opened, with 응. 고마워 is what you say to a friend; 감사합니다 would be for someone you are not on 반말 terms with in the first place.
items.grammar: 고마워요 → 고마워. 고맙다 is ㅂ-irregular, like 맵다 in 연습 2: the ㅂ becomes 우 in front of a vowel, so 고맙 + 어 = 고마워, and 고맙어 is what it would be if the ㅂ held on.

example.en: Steven, is now a good time to talk?

exercises.blurbEn: I’m about to do this — do you want to come along?
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book prints a picture and one long blank for the whole of A’s line. Here the phrase to work from is printed above the row and the two verb forms are the choices, because those are the two decisions in it: -(으)려고 하다 for what you are about to do, and -(으)ㄹ래요 for whether the other person wants in. Both take 으 after a consonant and nothing after a vowel. And look at the [보기] before assuming the two verbs are the same one — you boil the ramyeon, and what you ask about is the eating.

items.en: A: I’m thinking of going to see a film — do you want to come? — B: Yes, I’d like that.
items.why: A is not asking whether B will go to the cinema in general; A has a plan and is opening it up. That is the whole shape of the sentence: -(으)려고 하는데 lays the plan down, and -(으)ㄹ래요 hands the decision over.
items.grammar: 가다 → 가려고, 갈래요. The stem ends in a vowel, so no 으 goes in front of either ending, and in 갈래요 the ㄹ attaches straight to 가. 가려고 is intending to go; 가러 is not Korean, because -(으)러 only ever pairs with 가다, 오다 and 다니다 — which is exactly what 보러 가다 is doing earlier in this same line.

lines.ko: 저는 운동하는 걸 별로 안 좋아해요.

items.en: A: I’m thinking of learning taekwondo — do you want to learn with me? — B: I’m not all that keen on doing sport.
items.why: The first refusal on the page, and it refuses without ever saying no: B says what they are like rather than what they will do. 별로 is the adverb that lives with a negative — 별로 안 좋아해요, not much — and 걸 is 것을, the shortest way to make 운동하다 into something you can dislike.
items.grammar: 배우다 → 배우려고, 배울래요. Another vowel stem, so no 으 either time. 배울려고 is what a lot of people say out loud, and it is not the standard form: the ㄹ belongs to -(으)ㄹ래요 and has no business in -(으)려고.

items.en: A: I’m about to have lunch — do you want to eat with me? — B: I ate with a friend a little while ago.
items.why: The one consonant stem on the page, so the one row where the 으 has to be there. B turns it down with a fact rather than an opinion — already eaten — and 랑 is the spoken 와/과: 친구랑, with a friend.
items.grammar: 먹다 → 먹으려고, 먹을래요. 먹 ends in ㄱ, so both endings need the 으 to get started: 먹려고 and 먹래요 are what the vowel stems give and this stem cannot. Compare 가려고 and 갈래요 in item 1, where there is no 으 at all.

items.en: A: I’m going to take a walk — do you want to come? — B: Yes, I’d like that.
items.why: Worth reading the answer twice: the second half is 할래요, not 산책할래요. Once the plan has been said there is no need to name it again, so 하다 stands in for the whole thing — which is what 하다 is for.
items.grammar: 산책하다 → 산책하려고, and then 할래요 on its own. 하 is a vowel stem, so no 으 goes in; 산책하러 would need a 가다 or an 오다 after it — 산책하러 나가다 — and there is none here.

lines.ko: 전 테니스를 전혀 칠 줄 몰라요.

items.en: A: I’m thinking of playing tennis — do you want to play with me? — B: I can’t play tennis at all.
items.why: The flattest refusal of the three: not unwilling but unable. V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다[모르다] is knowing how to do something, and 전혀 is the 별로 of item 2 turned all the way up — it too only ever appears with a negative.
items.grammar: 치다 → 치려고, 칠래요. The stem is the single vowel 치, so the ㄹ of -(으)ㄹ래요 lands right on it: 칠래요. And note B’s 칠 줄 — the same ㄹ, doing the same thing in front of 줄.

example.en: A: I’m about to boil some ramyeon — want to eat with me? — B: Yes, I’d like that.

exercises.blurbEn: Two pictures, one choice: A offers the first, B talks you into the second.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Two pictures side by side and you choose between them: A asks about the first, B gives a reason and proposes the second. All of it is 반말, which is why this page comes after 문법과 표현 2 — the question is -(으)ㄹ래 with no 요 and the answer is -자. Watch what -(으)니까 is doing there as well: it is the reason clause a suggestion has to use, because -아/어서 cannot stand in front of -자. The book’s fifth row is two question marks — invent your own pair — and nothing can mark that, so the four the key answers are the four here.

items.en: A: Shall we take a taxi home? — B: The roads are jammed, so let’s take the subway.
items.why: B does not turn the taxi down and stop there — the reason comes first and then the alternative, which is the shape of every row on this page. 길이 막히다 is the roads being blocked, and it is the standard reason for choosing the subway in Seoul.
items.grammar: 가다 → 갈래, and 타다 → 타자. -(으)ㄹ래 is -(으)ㄹ래요 with the 요 taken off, the same as everything on the 반말 page. 탑시다 says the same thing as 타자 but in the formal style, so it does not belong in a conversation like this one.

items.en: A: Shall we go to the department store for a present? — B: Department stores are expensive, so let’s go to the market.
items.why: 사러 is the -(으)러 that item 1 of 연습 1 said only goes with 가다 and 오다 — and here it is, in front of 갈래. B’s reason is the price, so the answer moves from the 백화점 to the 시장 rather than dropping the errand.
items.grammar: 갈래 asks what you want; 갈게 promises what I will do, and a promise cannot be a question. They share the -(으)ㄹ and are told apart by nothing but 래 against 게, which is why they get mixed up.

items.en: A: Do you want to go hiking this weekend? — B: Hiking is hard work, so let’s go to the sea.
items.why: The mountain against the sea, which is the whole of a Korean summer weekend. 등산 is hiking as a noun, so it takes 하다 to become something you can do, and B reuses the same noun as the subject of the reason.
items.grammar: Look at B’s printed line: 힘들다 + -(으)니까 comes out as 힘드니까, not 힘들으니까 — a ㄹ stem drops its ㄹ in front of ㄴ. It is the same drop as 만들다 → 만드니까 and 살다 → 사니까.

items.en: A: Do you want a coffee? — B: I’ve already had coffee, so let’s get an ice cream.
items.why: The only row where A’s line is nothing but the offer, and the only one whose reason is in the past: 아까 마셨으니까, because I drank some earlier. 아까 is a little while ago — near enough to still count.
items.grammar: 마시다 → 마실래, and 먹다 → 먹자. -자 goes straight onto the stem and never takes 으, however the stem ends: 먹자 and 가자, never 먹으자. That is what makes it different from -(으)ㄹ래 and -(으)려고, which both need the 으 after 먹.

example.en: A: Do you want galbitang for lunch? — B: It’s hot out, so let’s have naengmyeon.

exercises.blurbEn: This one yes, that one no — and the joining form depends on the word.
exercises.instructionKo: 그림을 보고 [보기]와 같이 문장을 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Look at the pictures and complete each sentence as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Two pictures a row, and one sentence that turns on the contrast between them. Items 1 to 4 print everything except the joining form; the book leaves 5 and 6 blank from end to end, so the two nouns are printed here and both halves are yours. The form is the lesson: a verb takes -는데, an adjective takes -(으)ㄴ데, a noun takes -인데 — and anything in the past takes -는데 whatever it started out as. Item 4 is where that bites, because 좋다 is an adjective and still comes out 좋았는데.

items.en: I eat beef, but I don’t eat pork.
items.why: The same dish twice over, made of different meat, and the sentence says yes to one and no to the other. 는 on both nouns is what marks them as the two sides of it — 소고기는 … 돼지고기는.
items.grammar: 먹다 is a verb, so the joining form is -는데: 먹 + 는데. -(으)ㄴ데 is the adjective one, which is why 먹은데 is not a form at all, and -는데 goes straight onto the stem with no 으 in front of it.

lines.ko: 저는 부산은 {} 제주도는 안 가 봤어요.

items.en: I’ve been to Busan, but I haven’t been to Jeju.
items.why: V-아/어 보다 is having tried something or been somewhere, and the second half repeats it in the negative — 안 가 봤어요 — so the first half has to be in the past as well.
items.grammar: 가 봤다 → 가 봤는데. Once 았/었 is in the stem the ending is -는데, whatever the word underneath was, so there is no such thing as an -(으)ㄴ데 after a past tense.

items.phraseKo: 나나 씨 집 / 켈리 씨 집

lines.ko: 나나 씨 집은 학교에서 {} 켈리 씨 집은 멀어요.

items.en: Nana’s place is near the school, but Kelly’s is far.
items.why: 가깝다 and 멀다 are the two halves, near and far, and 학교에서 is the point both are measured from — 에서 for the place you are measuring out of, as on the N 중에(서) page.
items.grammar: 가깝다 is an adjective, so -(으)ㄴ데 — and it is ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ turns into 우 before the vowel of the ending: 가깝 + 은데 = 가까운데. The same change as 맵다 → 매운 on the 어휘 page.

items.en: The weather was nice yesterday, but today it’s raining.
items.why: Here the two sides are two days rather than two things. 오네요 is the -네요 of the 반말 page — noticing something as you say it — which is what makes the rain sound like news.
items.grammar: 좋다 is an adjective and would be 좋은데 in the present. In the past it is 좋았는데, because 았/었 takes -는데. That is the one thing worth carrying out of this page: the tense decides the ending before the word class gets a say.

items.en: I like comedies, but I’m not that keen on scary films.
items.why: The book leaves this row blank from one end to the other, so both halves are yours: the joining form on 좋아하다, and a second half that has to disagree with the first. 별로 is the word for not much, and it only ever turns up with a negative.
items.grammar: 좋아하다 → 좋아하는데, a verb like any other. In the second half 안 sits immediately in front of the verb — 별로 안 좋아해요 — and never in front of the adverb. Note the spelling too: -는데 ends in 데, while -는대 is the quotative, reporting what somebody else said.

items.en: I drink green tea often, but I don’t drink coffee much.
items.why: The same shape as item 5 with the adverb doing the work instead of the verb: 자주 on both sides and the negative on one of them. Take the negative out and the sentence contradicts nothing, which is the one thing -는데 is here to do.
items.grammar: 마시다 → 마시는데. -는데 goes on the plain stem, so 마셔는데 is the 아/어 form where it has no business being — the same mistake as 추워지 for 춥지 on the 반말 page. And again 안 goes right in front of the verb: 자주 안 마셔요.

example.en: I’m good at football, but I can’t play basketball.

exercises.blurbEn: Yes to half of it — and two irregulars hiding in the joining forms.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 대화를 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each dialogue as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: All of it 반말, and every answer takes one side of the question before turning it. The forms are the exercise: -는데 after a verb, -(으)ㄴ데 after an adjective, -는데 after anything in the past. Two of the five hide an irregular — 덥다 loses its ㅂ, 알다 loses its ㄹ — and one hides its tense in A’s line rather than B’s.

items.en: A: Nana, didn’t you sleep well last night? — B: No, I slept fine — but I’m tired.
items.why: A guesses that Nana slept badly, so 아니 is answering the question rather than the tiredness: she did sleep well. Then the turn — well slept and tired all the same.
items.grammar: 자다 → 잤는데. 자 + 았 has nowhere to go but together, giving 잤, and the past takes -는데. 자는데 is the present, which cannot go with the 어제 in A’s question.

items.en: A: What’s the weather like in Busan these days? — B: A bit hot in the daytime, but the mornings and evenings are cool.
items.why: 낮 against 아침, 저녁 — the contrast is inside a single day rather than between two things. 좀 softens it the way it always does: a bit hot, not hot.
items.grammar: 덥다 is an adjective, so -(으)ㄴ데, and it is ㅂ-irregular: 덥 + 은데 = 더운데. Not 덥은데, and not 더워는데 either — 더워 is the 아/어 form and -는데 does not go on it.

lines.ko: 샤오밍, 저 가수 노래 정말 잘하지?
노래는 {} 춤은 잘 못 추는 것 같아.

items.en: A: Xiaoming, that singer really can sing, can’t they? — B: They can sing, but I don’t think they can dance.
items.why: A asks with -지, which is asking to be agreed with, and B agrees with half of it. 노래는 … 춤은 is the same 는 … 는 pairing as 연습 1, and 것 같아 keeps the second half a guess rather than a verdict.
items.grammar: 잘하다 → 잘하는데, a verb. Note 춤을 추다 for dancing — Korean dances a dance — so the negative lands on 추다: 잘 못 추는 것 같아.

lines.ko: 스티븐, 네 친구 에도도 한국말 잘해?

items.en: A: Steven, is your friend Edo good at Korean as well? — B: No — he lived in Korea a long time, but he isn’t.
items.why: The contrast is between what living here a long time would lead you to expect and what is actually the case. 네 친구 is the 네 of the 반말 page, and the 도 in 에도도 is the particle — Edo too — sitting on a name that happens to end the same way.
items.grammar: 살다 → 살았는데 in the past. In the present it would be 사는데, because a ㄹ stem drops its ㄹ in front of the ㄴ of -는데; 살는데 is that drop left undone. The past sidesteps the question, since 았 + 는데 has no ㄹ left to decide about.

lines.ko: 아니, 읽을 줄은 {} 쓸 줄은 몰라.

items.en: A: Can you write hanja? — B: No — I can read it, but I can’t write it.
items.why: V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알다[모르다] is knowing how to do something, the same phrase as 칠 줄 몰라요 on the V-(으)ㄹ래요 page. 읽을 줄은 … 쓸 줄은 puts 는 on both, so the contrast is between the reading and the writing rather than between the knowing and the not.
items.grammar: 알다 → 아는데. The ㄹ drops in front of the ㄴ of -는데: 알 + 는데 = 아는데, the same drop as 살다 → 사는데 and 만들다 → 만드는데. 알은데 keeps the ㄹ and takes the adjective ending as well, so it is wrong twice over.

lines.ko: 아니, 열심히 {} 생각보다 잘 못 봤어.

example.en: A: Julien, did the exam go well? — B: No — I studied hard, but it went worse than I expected.

exercises.blurbEn: Each opening sets you up. Find the half that lets you down.
exercises.instructionKo: [보기]와 같이 문장을 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Complete each sentence as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The book prints the first half and leaves the rest of the line to you, with one model answer in the key and a fifth row with nothing printed at all. Writing cannot be marked, so the four endings the key gives are shuffled here and each goes back to the opening it contradicts. That pairing is what the exercise is actually after: -는데 sets up an expectation and the second half defies it. Two of the openings are the same 먹었는데, so what tells them apart is which ending would be a surprise after it.

items.en: It’s exam period, but I haven’t been able to study much.
items.why: Exam weeks are when you would expect someone to be at their books, so the half that turns it has to be the studying that did not happen. 기간 is a stretch of time — 시험 기간, the weeks the exams run.
items.grammar: 기간 is a noun, so the form is -인데: 기간 + 인데, which is 이다 with -는데 on it. That is the N인데 in the heading of this page. And 못 했어요 is could not rather than did not — the difference between being stopped and choosing.

items.en: I took medicine, but it still hurts.
items.why: Medicine is for stopping the hurting, so still hurting is exactly what does not follow from it. 아직도 is the still that goes with something you had every reason to expect to be over.
items.grammar: 약을 먹다 — Korean eats medicine rather than taking it. 먹었는데 is past, so -는데. And 아프다 → 아파요: the ㅡ drops in front of 아/어, and the syllable in front decides which one, so 아프 + 아요 = 아파요.

items.en: I ate a lot at lunch, but I’m hungry.
items.why: The other side of the same coin as item 2: a big lunch is the reason not to be hungry. Both openings are 먹었는데, and the only thing that tells them apart is which ending would be a surprise after it.
items.grammar: 배고프다 → 배고파요, the same ㅡ-irregular as 아프다 in item 2. 배가 고프다 is the stomach being hungry, and 배고프다 is those two words run together into one.

items.en: I called my friend, but they didn’t pick up.
items.why: You ring someone in order that they answer, so not answering is the turn. 받다 is what a phone call takes in Korean — 전화를 받다, to pick up.
items.grammar: 하다 → 했는데: 하 + 였 gives 했, and then -는데 because it is past. 한테 is the spoken to-a-person from the 반말 page, and 안 goes right in front of the verb: 안 받았어요.

example.en: It’s winter, but it isn’t particularly cold.

exercises.blurbEn: Three words from the teacher, one superlative back — out loud.
exercises.instructionKo: 잘 듣고 [보기]와 같이 대답해 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Listen and answer as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The teacher reads three words — the group, the winner, the adjective — and leaves four seconds for you to build the sentence. The clip on each row is that exchange with the four seconds taken out, so it runs about nine rather than fourteen. Two decisions are yours: which subject particle the winner takes, and the 반말 form of the adjective. The answers are 반말 throughout, which is what the [보기] on the recording establishes.

items.en: Of all flowers, roses are the prettiest.
items.why: The three words come in the order the sentence needs them: the group first, then the one that wins, then what it wins at. Only the particles and the ending are left to you.
items.grammar: 장미 ends in a vowel, so the subject particle is 가. And 예쁘다 → 예뻐: the ㅡ drops in front of 아/어, and with no syllable in front to borrow a vowel from it defaults to 어. 예쁜 is the form that goes before a noun, not the one that ends a sentence.

items.en: Of all Korean songs, this one is the best.
items.why: The group and the winner are almost the same words here — 한국 노래 against 이 노래 — which is what makes it worth saying twice: the set, then the one out of it.
items.grammar: 노래 ends in a vowel, so 가 again. 좋다 → 좋아, because 좋 has ㅗ in it and takes 아; 좋어 is the same slip as writing 좋어요.

items.en: Monday is the busiest day of the week.
items.why: A week is a set of days the same way a bunch of flowers is a set of flowers, which is what 일주일 중에서 says. This is the 1년 중에서 of the 문법과 표현 page at a smaller scale.
items.grammar: 월요일 ends in the consonant ㄹ, so the particle is 이 and not 가. 바쁘다 → 바빠: the ㅡ drops and this time there is a syllable in front with ㅏ in it, so the ending is 아. Compare 예뻐 in item 1, where there was not.

lines.ko: 우리 반 학생, 샤오밍 씨, 멋있다

items.en: Xiaoming is the coolest person in our class.
items.why: The same group as 연습 1 of the 문법과 표현 page — 우리 반 학생 — and the same shape of answer. 멋있다 is said of a person who has style rather than looks.
items.grammar: 씨 ends in a vowel, so 가. 멋있다 → 멋있어: it is built on 있다, so the vowel is 어, never 아. That 있다 is also why the form in front of a noun would be 멋있는 — the same exception as 맛있는 two pages back.

example.en: T: Korean food, bibimbap, tasty — S: Bibimbap is the tastiest Korean food.

exercises.blurbEn: The teacher asks it politely. You ask it again as a friend would.
exercises.instructionKo: 잘 듣고 [보기]와 같이 반말로 바꿔 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Listen and change each question into 반말 as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The shortest exchanges on the track: one question in 해요체 and the same question in 반말. The teacher’s line is printed above each row, so leaving the 요 on is not a matter of taste here — the row asks for the change and one of the three forms has not made it. Two rows hide something under the 요: 듣다 is ㄷ-irregular, and 거예요 does not simply lose a syllable.

items.en: Do you listen to music often?
items.why: A yes-or-no question, and in 반말 nothing marks it as one except the tone of voice — which is exactly what the recording is for.
items.grammar: 듣다 → 들어. The ㄷ turns into ㄹ in front of a vowel ending, so 듣 + 어 gives 들어 and never 듣어. The 해요체 form 들어요 has already done that change; the row only takes the 요 off it.

items.en: Is your place far from here?
items.why: 여기서 is 여기에서 worn down, which is what happens to 에서 in speech all the time. 멀다 is the 멀어요 of the -는데 page, met again with nothing on it.
items.grammar: 멀다 → 멀어. It is pronounced 머러, because the ㄹ moves across to the next syllable when you say it, but the ㄹ stays where it belongs in writing.

items.en: What did you do last weekend?
items.why: A question word rather than a yes-or-no this time — 뭐 is 무엇 in speech. 지난 주말 is last weekend, as against 이번 주말, this one.
items.grammar: 했어요 → 했어. 하다 takes 여 rather than 아/어, and 하 + 였 contracts to 했, so 하었어 is a form that never exists.

items.en: Where are you going for the holidays?
items.why: 방학 is the school holidays rather than a holiday you take, and 이번 방학 is the one coming. The question is about a plan, which is what -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is for.
items.grammar: 거예요 → 거야, because 거예요 is 거 + 이에요 and 이에요 becomes 이야 — contracted to 야 after the vowel of 거. Dropping the 요 on its own would leave 거예, which is not a word.

example.en: T: What time do you get up? — S: What time do you get up?

exercises.blurbEn: A time, a place, a verb — turn it into an invitation.
exercises.instructionKo: 잘 듣고 [보기]와 같이 대답해 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Listen and answer as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: Three words again, and this time the particle is the whole difficulty: which one the place takes depends on the verb at the end. 가다 and 오다 take 에 for where you are going, 만나다 takes 에서 for where the meeting happens, and 먹다 takes 을/를 because what you eat is an object rather than a place. The time word takes 에 on every row.

items.en: Shall we go to Jeju for the holidays?
items.why: The same island as the 문법과 표현 pages, and the same 이번 방학 as 연습 2. Going somewhere makes it a destination, so it takes 에.
items.grammar: 제주도에 갈래요. 에서 would be where something happens — 제주도에서 수영할래요 — and 가다 has no object, so 제주도를 is not available either. 갈게요 promises rather than asks, which is why it cannot end a question.

items.en: Shall we meet in front of the school this evening?
items.why: The one row that takes 에서, and the verb is why: meeting is something that happens at a place rather than movement towards one. 학교 앞 is a place made of two nouns, like 학교 근처 on the N 중에(서) page.
items.grammar: 만나다 → 만날래요, a vowel stem, so the ㄹ lands straight on 나. And 에서 for where an action happens: 학교 앞에서 만나요, 학교 앞에 가요.

items.en: Do you want to come to mine on Sunday?
items.why: 오다 rather than 가다, because the speaker is already where the listener would be coming to. 우리 집 is my place — Korean says our house for the one you live in, whoever else lives there.
items.grammar: 오다 → 올래요: a vowel stem, so no 으 goes in. 오을래요 spells out an 으 that only a consonant stem takes, as in 먹을래요 on the next row.

items.en: Shall we have bibimbap for lunch?
items.why: The middle word is not a place at all on this row, which is the point of putting it last: the particle follows what the word is and what the verb wants, not where it sits in the list.
items.grammar: 비빔밥 is what gets eaten, so it takes the object particle 을 — a consonant ending, so 을 rather than 를. And 먹다 is a consonant stem, so 먹을래요 with the 으 that 올래요 and 갈래요 do without.

example.en: T: weekend, library, go — S: Shall we go to the library at the weekend?

exercises.blurbEn: Two sentences in, one sentence out — joined at the contrast.
exercises.instructionKo: 잘 듣고 [보기]와 같이 한 문장으로 만들어 보세요.
exercises.instructionEn: Listen and join the two sentences into one, as shown in the example.
exercises.noteEn: The teacher reads two finished sentences and you fold them into one at the joining form. Because the first sentence is printed with its tense on it, there is nothing to guess: the form follows what you were given. Two of the four are the irregulars from the 문법과 표현 page — 가깝다 loses its ㅂ, 알다 loses its ㄹ — and the last one is past, which takes -는데 whatever the word class.

items.en: I like kimchi, but I don’t like kimchi stew.
items.why: The two dishes of the 어휘 pages set against each other: liking the ingredient and not the dish made of it. The second sentence comes across whole, negative and all.
items.grammar: 좋아하다 is a verb, so -는데. The teacher says 좋아해요 in the present, so 좋아했는데 would be putting a tense in that was not given, and 좋아하은데 uses the adjective ending on a verb.

items.en: The bus stop is close, but the subway station is far.
items.why: Near and far again, as on the 문법과 표현 page, with a bus stop and a station instead of two houses. 지하철역 is a Unit 10 word — the station the 맛집 was five minutes from.
items.grammar: 가깝다 is an adjective, so -(으)ㄴ데, and the ㅂ becomes 우 in front of it: 가까운데. The teacher’s 가까워요 has already made that change — 가까워 is 가깝 + 어 — so hearing it is the clue.

items.en: I know the face, but I don’t know the name.
items.why: Knowing someone by sight and not by name — 얼굴은 알다 is the set phrase for it. 모르다 is its own word rather than a negative of 알다, which is why the second half changes verb entirely.
items.grammar: 알다 → 아는데: the ㄹ drops in front of the ㄴ of -는데. The same drop as 살다 → 사는데, and the same row as 연습 2 of the 문법과 표현 page, which is where this one comes from.

lines.ko: 아침에는 비가 왔어요. 지금은 안 와요.

items.en: It rained this morning, but it isn’t raining now.
items.why: The only row whose two halves are in different tenses, and the contrast is between them: rain then, none now. 비가 오다 is how Korean says it rains — the rain comes.
items.grammar: 왔다 → 왔는데. 오 + 았 contracts to 왔, and a past tense takes -는데 whatever it was built on. 오는데 is the present, which the teacher’s 왔어요 rules out.

example.en: T: I’m good at football. I’m not good at basketball. — S: I’m good at football, but not at basketball.
